name: Investment Banking
summary: Banks advise companies, governments and investors on mergers and acquisitions and help them raise money by issuing debt and equity. They earn fees for finding investors and structuring deals.

guide.heading: How a bank is organised
items: Main divisions: Investment Banking (IBD), Sales & Trading, and Research. IBD is walled off from the rest of the firm ("the Wall").
Industry (coverage) groups: Consumer/Retail, Tech/Media/Telecom (TMT), Industrials, Natural Resources, Financial Institutions (FIG), Healthcare, Real Estate, Gaming & Lodging (REGL), and more.
Product groups: M&A, Equity Capital Markets (IPOs, secondary offerings), Debt Capital Markets (refinancing, restructuring, acquisition debt), Leveraged Finance (high-yield debt).
Life of a deal: pitching (industry groups with product support; pitch books, modeling and valuation), then execution (industry and product groups together), then follow-ups.
Hierarchy: Analyst (2–3 years), Associate, Vice President (where the job shifts to clients), Director, Managing Director.

guide.heading: Types of banks
items: Bulge bracket: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JP Morgan, Bank of America, Citi, Barclays, UBS, Wells Fargo.
Middle market: Jefferies, Raymond James, Harris Williams, HSBC, BNP Paribas, Houlihan Lokey.
Elite boutiques: Evercore, Greenhill, Lazard, Moelis, Perella Weinberg, Centerview.

guide.heading: The analyst role
items: Financial modeling in Excel, building pitch books, presenting ideas to senior bankers, and working with clients and executives.
Long hours, especially on live deals; a typical day runs from about 9 a.m. to midnight.

Why IB: a strong foundation in modeling and valuation, deals with tangible results, C-suite exposure, a strong network, and exits to private equity, venture capital, hedge funds, development finance, corporate finance, or promotion to Associate.

guide.heading: How to get the job
items: Network: cold calls, coffee chats and info sessions.
Interviews: HireVue, then a first round (phone or on campus), then a Superday of 3–5 back-to-back interviews.
Know every common behavioral question. For technicals, the M&I 400 guide covers most topics.

guide.heading: Technical questions to know
items: The 3 main ways to value a company, and which gives the highest and lowest values. Other valuation methods.
What is investment banking? How do product and coverage groups work together?
Walk through how a change in one balance-sheet account flows through the statements. What is working capital?
Walk me through a DCF (WACC, CAPM). What is Beta?
What is EBITDA and why is it used? What is an LBO?
Enterprise value vs. equity value, and how to calculate each. Debt vs. equity.

guide.heading: IB vs. Sales & Trading
items: Hours: banking about 9 a.m.–1 a.m. with weekend work; trading about 7 a.m.–6 p.m. with weekends off.
Culture: in banking, reputation is built on endurance; in trading, on results.
Work: banking is project-based and quiet; trading is continuous (you manage your book), loud and fast.

name: Consulting
summary: Consultants give expert advice to organizations to improve performance and make hard decisions, creating value through revenue growth, cost savings, M&A and other advisory work.

guide.heading: What the work looks like
items: Firms advise most blue-chip companies across industries. Many management consultancies are industry-agnostic; boutiques specialize by industry, function or region.
Projects (cases) usually last 3–6 months and are renewed monthly; long-term clients may sign multi-year contracts. Work happens at the client site or in the office.
Expect 50–60 hour weeks, with weekends protected.
Types of work: management, strategy, M&A, operations, HR, tech/IT, risk & compliance, supply chain, sustainability, and more.

Example roles on a case: the Partner wins the work and sets the approach; the Manager runs client meetings, the timeline and sub-teams; the Analyst gathers and analyzes data, builds clear visuals and brings recommendations to the manager.

guide.heading: Major firms
items: MBB ("Big Three"): McKinsey, BCG and Bain, the most prestigious management consulting firms.
Big Four: Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG, best known for tax and audit, with large consulting arms.
Specialized boutiques: industry- or service-specific firms.

guide.heading: Why consulting
items: Exposure to many industries and frequent C-suite interaction; travel perks at global firms.
Real responsibility as a junior analyst; builds speaking, Excel modeling and strategy skills.
Funded graduate school, a lifelong network and strong exits: corporate strategy, senior management, MBA/law school, PE/VC/hedge funds, entrepreneurship, tech, international development, non-profits.
These jobs are very hard to get: firms hire fewer than 1% of applicants.

guide.heading: What firms look for
items: Coachability, a hard-working attitude, and meaningful experiences with clear personal impact.
Clear communication and public speaking; teamwork, leadership and initiative.
Structured problem solving and quantitative reasoning; intellectual curiosity.
Personability and the ability to build trust (the "airport test").

guide.heading: Online assessments
items: McKinsey Solve: game-based problems testing analytical reasoning, decisions and adaptability; evaluated alongside the application.
Bain TestGorilla: timed questions on analysis, problem solving and communication; one data point and a smaller factor.
BCG Casey: a chatbot-led case testing quantitative reasoning, exhibit analysis and recommendations; an evaluative stage.
Aim for the 9th or 10th decile on Solve and Casey; lower scores make it harder to progress.

guide.heading: Case interviews
items: Tests how you think, communicate and solve problems; typically 20–40 minutes. Format and length vary by firm.
Main types: profitability, market sizing, market entry, M&A.
New formats: digital cases (BCG Casey) and AI-assisted interviews where you work with an AI tool. Independent reasoning, checking outputs and explaining your recommendation still matter.
McKinsey is piloting a simulated client conversation: handle ambiguity and pushback, ask useful questions, and show empathy. It was non-evaluative in the 2026 cycle, with wider use expected.

guide.heading: Resources
items: CaseCoach (free through Vanderbilt), Management Consulted, PrepLounge, CaseInterview.com, Crafting Cases, RocketBlocks, and firms' own prep pages.
MBA case books for practice cases.
Vanderbilt Career Center / Handshake; levels.fyi for salaries; Fishbowl for industry forums.

guide.heading: Entry-level base pay (figures from the Oct 2026 slides)
items: MBB: McKinsey $125k, BCG $125k, Bain $120k.
Big Four: Deloitte $84–95k, KPMG $78–94k, EY up to $90k, PwC up to $90k.
Others: Oliver Wyman $110k, Alvarez & Marsal up to $112k, Accenture Strategy $105k, EY-Parthenon $100k, L.E.K. $95k.

name: Tech, Trading & Frontier AI
summary: Big Tech builds software, hardware and digital infrastructure at scale; quantitative trading firms use math, statistics and code to trade systematically; frontier AI labs push the state of the art in AI research.

guide.heading: Roles
items: Tech: Software Engineer (designs, builds and maintains systems; not programming all day), Product Manager (sets strategy and priorities across engineering, design and business), UI/UX Designer (research, interface design, prototyping, usability testing).

Trading: Quant Trader (runs strategies, manages risk and inventory), Quant Researcher (finds predictive signals with statistics and ML), Quant Developer (builds research and trading systems), Trading Systems Engineer (low-latency infrastructure).
Frontier AI labs: Member of Technical Staff (MTS), a broad role on 10–14 week projects whose priorities shift quickly; high-risk, high-reward.

guide.heading: Hours, pay and location (figures from the Nov 2026 slides)
items: Tech: 30–45 hours a week, usually hybrid, weekends protected; entry-level total compensation $150k–$250k (base + stock); mostly California.
Trading: 45–50 hours a week on desk, weekends protected; entry-level TC $350k–$1.1M (base + bonus); mostly Chicago and NYC.
AI labs: 50–60 hours a week, usually on desk; entry-level TC $200k–$600k (base, equity and stock); mostly California.
Generally excellent benefits across all three. For pay: Quant > Frontier AI > Big Tech.

guide.heading: How recruiting works
items: Big Tech recruits starting late summer going into junior year: typically 2–3 technical rounds and 1–2 behavioral, including a superday.
Quant recruits starting late spring at the end of sophomore year: up to 8 technical rounds, usually at most 1 behavioral, with an in-person superday.
AI labs and startups recruit at any time; processes vary widely.
Most people apply with just a resume and a referral; cover letters are rare. A referral helps you get the first interview, and after that only your ability matters.

guide.heading: How to get good
items: It takes time, and lots of it.
Technical interviews test two things: getting the answer right, and how you think: approaching problems sensibly, explaining your reasoning and showing you're coachable.
Behavioral interviews are where you stand out: be reasonable, rational and sociable.
Example: given a dataset and an LLM, explore the data, form ideas and use the LLM to build models quickly.

Example: a fair coin is flipped 1000 times (+$1 heads, −$1 tails) and you can stop any time. How do you maximize profit? What is the chance you're ever at +$3? What if the coin is biased, or the bias is unknown?

guide.heading: Resources
items: Levels.fyi (salaries), LeetCode (coding interviews), Quantable (quant interviews), APMList.com (product roles).
Reddit: r/csMajors and r/quantfinance.
Internship trackers: github.com/SimplifyJobs (Summer internships) and github.com/northwesternfintech (quant internships).
